job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Esther Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did software engineering at Glasgow, and since September I've been a junior developer at an insurance company, working on the system that handles home insurance claims. I use an AI coding assistant for pretty much everything, and then I read every line it gives me twice. I rent a room with two friends from church, I sing in the choir on Wednesdays, and on Saturdays I do free website help for a charity shop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a claim that used to take a week goes through in an hour, because I know somebody's kitchen is getting fixed faster. What wears me out is that nobody on my team is under thirty-five, so I'm always the one who has to ask. I owe about 20,000, and I have about seven weeks of spending saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, a bit of breathing space. I'd also say hype or not, I'll still use it every day, because it makes me faster than the others on my team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit bored. I like the idea of being at the front of something big. But my job and money feel safe, and the insurance firm isn't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and use the quiet to start my own project. I'd build a simple booking and donations tool for churches and charities, charge a small monthly fee, and see if I can get ten customers in a year. I'd also put 250 a month on my loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Steady, and a bit ambitious. It's the best version for starting something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why churches and charities?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they're in my life, and I see how much time the volunteers waste on spreadsheets. I'd rather sell something useful to people I know than something clever to people I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family think of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, who fixes buses, says a job with a pension is better than a risk. My mum, a carer, says work hard and don't borrow. I'll listen to both and still try it.

say: I'd say good, a bit of **breathing space**, and I'll still use AI every day because it makes me faster.
I'd tell friends to build **something of their own**.
think: Privately I'd be a bit **bored**, because I like being at the front of something big.
My job and money feel **safe**, and the insurance firm isn't going anywhere.
do: Build a booking and donations tool for **churches and charities** and aim for ten customers.
Put **250 a month** on my loan and keep my job.
feel: **Steady** and a bit ambitious; it's the best version for starting something.
S0.quote: I'd rather sell something useful to people I know than something clever to people I don't.
fieldNote: She treats a quiet world as a **chance to start something**, which suits her adaptive streak.
Her business idea comes from **church volunteers**, drawing on her community.
Her parents give opposite advice, and she plans to hear both.

steps.text: Keep working on the claims system at the insurer
Build a booking and donations tool for churches and aim for ten customers
Put 250 a month towards the student loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get on board or get left behind. At the insurer, I'd tell my team to use the tools properly and not be shy about it. I'd also say firms should let people keep their jobs and learn, not just cut them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is exactly what the card says, coding and answering customers, so I'm a bit uneasy. But I'm the one on my team who knows how to use the tools best, so I think I'm more likely to be kept. The people over forty on my team are the ones I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to run a short session for my team on how I use the tools, because being the person who teaches it is valuable. I'd speed up my side project, so I'd have a real customer by next spring. I'd also pick up a skill that needs talking to people, like leading a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. I'd rather be in the race than watching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't there a risk in helping colleagues who might compete with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But I'd rather be known as the person who helped than the person who hoarded. I'd feel awful watching people I like fall behind. It's also my way of being sure I'm part of the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the firm in return?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written promise that anyone who learns the tools won't be the first to be let go. I don't expect a guarantee, but I'd ask.

say: I'd say get on board or get left behind, and firms should let people **keep their jobs** and learn.
I'd tell my team to use the tools **properly**.
think: My job is coding and answering customers, so I'm a bit uneasy, but I know the tools **best**.
The people over forty on my team are the ones I'd **worry** about.
do: Run a short session for my team on **use the tools**.
Speed up my side project so I have a **real customer** by spring.
feel: **Uneasy but excited**; I'd rather be in the race than watching it.
S1.quote: I'd rather be known as the person who helped than the person who hoarded.
fieldNote: Her helpfulness is **community-minded**, and she is honest that it is also a way to secure her place.
She asks for a written promise from the firm, a **mild request** rather than a demand.
She worries about older colleagues, not herself.

steps.text: Run a lunchtime session for my team on how I use AI tools
Get one paying customer for the church booking tool by spring
Take a short project leadership course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast and I'd want communities, families and firms to hold together. I wouldn't want a big state programme, but I'd want employers to be honest. I'd say it in church and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be anxious, not frozen. If AI can do almost any thinking work in 2028, my job goes and my degree matters much less. The hands-on side holds for three more years, and I'm not hands-on. But I'd be one of the few people who already knows how to use it, so I'd try to get ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make my own business the main thing and treat the job as a bridge. I'd cut spending, build six months of savings, and talk to my pastor about which charities and churches need a tool like mine. I'd also ask my parents if I could move home for six months, which I don't like but it makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit like the day before an exam. I'd be praying more, and working harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum, the carer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm fine, and then she'd ask a question and I wouldn't be able to keep it up. She works with people at the end of their lives, so she knows what to say to someone who's scared. She'd tell me to eat something and call my gran.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your church for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd ask for customers and prayers. I'd rather build something people pay for than ask for handouts.

say: I'd say two years is too fast and I'd want **employers to be honest**.
I wouldn't want a big **state programme**; I'd want communities to hold together.
think: If AI does almost any thinking work in 2028, my **job goes** and my degree matters much less.
I'd be one of the few who already **know the tools**, so I'd try to get ahead.
do: Make my **own business** the main thing and treat the job as a bridge.
Move home for six months and build **six months** of savings.
feel: **Anxious**, like the day before an exam; I'd be praying more and working harder.
S2.quote: I'd rather build something people pay for than ask for handouts.
fieldNote: Her fear is real but she turns it into **a business plan**, in line with her free-market views.
Her mother, a carer, would see through her calm and tell her to **eat something**.
She refuses handouts even from the church and asks for customers.

steps.text: Make the church booking tool my main project and find ten customers
Move back to my parents' house for six months
Cut spending to the bone and build six months of savings
Put every spare pound towards the loan and a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let's use it. I'd say people should start businesses, learn the tools and save, and that employers should help them do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm cautiously excited. By 2031 I'd be 27, and I could have a real company with customers and maybe employees. Everyone else would be racing to learn the tools, so I'd have to find something that's more than the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow my side business into my main job within three years, hire a part-time person if I can, and save for a deposit. I'd get to know ten charities and churches really well, because trust is something AI can't fake. And I'd keep studying new tools every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a stomach flip. It's the one where I'd either do something big or do something sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would trust matter more than the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a church treasurer's giving data goes wrong, they won't ring a chatbot, they'll ring someone they know. I'd like to be that someone. It's the human bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the AI makes the tool for free?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd sell the setting up, the training and the knowing the people. The software might be free, but the sitting in the vestry and listening to what they need isn't.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair warning**, so people should start businesses and save.
I'd say employers should **help** them do it.
think: By 2031 I'd be 27 and could have a **real company** with customers.
I'd have to find something that's **more than the tools**.
do: Grow my side business into my **main job** within three years.
Get to know ten **charities and churches** well and keep studying new tools weekly.
feel: **Excited**, with a stomach flip; I'd do something big or something sensible.
S3.quote: If a church treasurer's giving data goes wrong, they won't ring a chatbot, they'll ring someone they know.
fieldNote: She bets on **trust and presence**, the things she thinks AI can't fake.
Her answer to free software is **service**: setup, training and listening.
She is uneasy rather than calm because the plan depends on her business working.

steps.text: Turn the booking tool into my main job within three years
Visit ten charities and churches to learn what they need
Try one new AI tool every week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a big gift. We should use it to teach children, support families and build things, and not wait for a government to tell us what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm calm. By 2036 I'd be 32, probably married and maybe with a child, and with my own company or a good senior job. I'd have ten years of using AI daily, so I'd be one of the experienced ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work at the insurer for two years, then go full-time on my own company if it's working. I'd save for a flat, get married to someone from church, and keep singing in the choir. I'd also teach teenagers at church to code on Saturdays, because that's how I'd help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and glad. It's the one where a person can have a normal life and be ambitious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the people who don't adapt as quickly as you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to help them, not rescue them. I'd run a class, share what I learned and tell them about jobs. If they'd rather not, that's their choice, but I wouldn't leave anyone behind without asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this one that scares you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that I get complacent. I like being ahead, and I'd hate to find out I'd stopped trying.

say: I'd say ten years is a **big gift**, and we should teach children and build things.
I'd say we shouldn't wait for a **government** to tell us what to do.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32, probably married, with my **own company** or a good senior job.
Ten years of daily AI use makes me one of the **experienced ones**.
do: Work at the insurer two years, then go **full-time** on my own company if it works.
Teach teenagers at church to **code** on Saturdays and save for a flat.
feel: **Calm**, and glad; a person can have a normal life and be ambitious.
S4.quote: I like being ahead, and I'd hate to find out I'd stopped trying.
fieldNote: Her one fear in the long scenario is **complacency**, an unusual and honest worry.
She would **help, not rescue** people who adapt more slowly, which fits her outlook.
Calm here because her work, money and faith all line up.

steps.text: Work at the insurer for two more years
Go full-time on my own company if it is working
Save for a flat and plan a church wedding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I wouldn't have time to build anything solid, and everyone around me would be scared at once. What would help is honest employers, a church and family around me, and customers for what I'm building. I'm not asking for handouts, I'm asking for a fair chance to build something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I know I sound confident, but I'm confident because I have people behind me. Take that away and I'd be a lot more frightened.

headlineQuote: I sound confident, but I'm confident because I have people behind me.
portrait: Esther is a 22-year-old **software engineer** in her first job at a Glasgow insurer, owing about 20,000.
She is adaptive, uses an **AI assistant** daily, and runs a booking tool idea for churches and charities.
Her traditional, free-market outlook means she wants a fair chance to build, not **handouts**, and leans on church and family.
She is calm at the plateau, anxious at two years, and **calm** again at ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most, because she'd have no time to build anything solid while everyone around her is scared.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest employers**, a church and family around her, and customers for what she is building.
